newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac poll appeal underwhelms French left, media.
newsitem.headline: Chirac poll appeal underwhelms French left, media.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac waded into France's tight parliamentary election race on Wednesday with a frontal assault on the record and platform of the left-wing opposition and an appeal for voters' trust and support.

"I need your support to continue the work we have begun together and which can only bear fruit over time. Let's seize our opportunity in a shared elan," he said in an article in 14 regional newspapers on the second anniversary of his election.
But an increasingly self-confident left brushed off Chirac's plea as nothing new, and many national and regional newspapers which were not invited to publish it took offence.
The conservative president defended his unpopular record and urged the French people not to turn their backs on history in the snap poll he has called on May 25 and June 1.

Latest opinion polls show the opposition Socialists and Communists level or edging ahead of his centre-right coalition in voting intentions, although the ruling alliance is still projected to win a majority in seats because of the two-round electoral system in single-member constituencies.
Accusing the left of wasteful tax-and-spend policies, Chirac urged voters to cast their ballots for the "political stability indispensible for effective action".

Polls published on Tuesday showed a massive 65 percent of voters were disappointed with Chirac's two years in office and felt his record was negative. A crushing 87 percent said his action had been negative in fighting unemployment.
Yet Chirac, seeking to give the flagging centre-right campaign a second wind, blamed the left for all France's ills.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin said blaming the left when the conservatives had been in power for four years was "surreal". He told France Inter radio that voters could have expected a higher vision and many would be disappointed.
Jospin said he would be penning a reply and would not discriminate among newspapers in distributing it.

He also sought to reassure voters and financial markets that if the left was elected, the Socialists would impose their pro-European line on a single European currency on their reluctant Communist allies.
"There won't be both a 'yes' and a 'no' to the single currency. There will be a single line, the one which (we) propose to the French people," Jospin said.
Markets were calm and the Paris Bourse CAC 40 index was up 0.3 percent in early trading.
Former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius added that Chirac's article was merely a "best of" compilation of his recent speeches bereft of any new ideas.
Centre-right UDF party leader Francois Leotard said he expected the president to intervene again in the campaign before the first round of voting.
Chirac said France had not always made the right choices and cited inefficient spending, a bloated public sector and high taxes, payroll charges and public debt.
Omitting any mention of unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe, he said the coalition elected in 1993 had been obliged to "wipe the slate clean" before making a new start.
He said the economy was now cleaned up and growth returning, ridiculing left-wing proposals to create hundreds of thousands of jobs in the public sector and order cuts in the working week.
Chirac sprinkled his appeal with buzzwords, some apparently borrowed from Britain's new prime minister, Tony Blair, and U.S. President Bill Clinton, such as "trust" and the 21st century.
Chirac phrased his article as an explicit appeal to voters to renew confidence in him two years after he took office.

His call took the same form as the announcement of his 1995 presidential candidacy, a regional newspaper article intended to go over the heads of the Paris media establishment and address provincial voters directly.
Most national dailies, irked that Chirac chose to ignore them, also published his article.

"Sorry, we got it too," the popular France-Soir exclaimed in a banner headline, saying that Chirac's communication advisers might be experts at selling washing powder but were "really hopeless as far as political intuition is concerned".
France-Inter radio joked: "There are those who have it, those who managed to get it, and those who could not and are very angry."
